items.title: Dozens Killed in Airstrikes Near Sudan-Egypt Border
items.summary: The attacks occurred at a remote gold mine hundreds of miles from the front lines of Sudan’s devastating civil war. Videos showed what appeared to be Egyptian munitions.
items.full_text:
Title: Dozens Killed in Airstrikes Near Sudan-Egypt Border - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/world/africa/egypt-sudan-goldmine-strike.html

Published Time: Mon, 12 Oct 2026 18:30:11 GMT

Markdown Content:
Dozens of gold workers in northern Sudan were killed over the weekend after warplanes bombed an open air mine near the Egyptian border, according to Sudanese rights groups, graphic video and eyewitnesses interviewed by The New York Times.

Footage from the aftermath of the bombing showed badly mutilated bodies of young men scattered amid sacks of mineral ore at a remote site in River Nile State, roughly 25 miles from Sudan’s border with Egypt.

“We were overcome with terror,” said Saif Eldin Adam, 26, a university student who worked at the mine for the past three months. Mr. Adam said he helped rescue the wounded and recover the dead after the strikes.

“There are no words for what we saw,” he said.

Emergency Lawyers, a rights group, estimated the death toll at 72. Two eyewitnesses said it was at least 65, with another 120 or more wounded.

The attack occurred hundreds of miles from the front lines of Sudan’s devastating civil war. Sudanese media [reports](https://sudantribune.com/article/319838) and several rights groups blamed the strike on Egypt. Last June, miners accused Egyptian forces of [carrying out a drone attack](https://sudantribune.com/article/315167) on another gold mine in the same region.

Sudan mines billions of dollars in gold every year, with the two warring sides using the profits to bankroll their fight. Sudan’s military has bombed mines controlled by its enemy, the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, in the far south of the country, in an effort to curtail a valuable source of finance.

The attack on Saturday was striking because it occurred in an army-controlled area largely untouched by fighting, and because the loudest accusations were directed at Egypt, a country that has been a staunch ally of Sudan’s military throughout the war.

In February, The Times revealed [a covert Egyptian drone base](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/01/world/africa/egypt-sudan-drones.html) that supported the Sudanese military’s war effort.

In a [statement](https://www.facebook.com/photo?fbid=1405730538398229&set=a.510305317940760&locale=ar_AR), Egypt’s military spokesman said its forces were in the third phase of “a major campaign to combat illegal gold prospecting in the Eastern Desert,” which came after leaflets were dropped to warn what he called “criminal elements.”

But the statement insisted that Egyptian forces had been acting inside their own borders, and not in Sudanese territory.

Sudan’s military avoided pointing fingers. On Monday the military chief, Gen. Abdul Fattah al-Burhan, announced an investigation into what he called a “painful incident.”

The bombing was notable in Sudan, even during an atrocity-laden conflict that has seen credible accusations of genocide, chemical weapons use, mass rape and starvation.

The targets of the strike appeared to be poor, largely young miners laboring in harsh conditions in a remote area. [Graphic footage](https://www.facebook.com/reel/28486385777697529) filmed in the [aftermath](https://www.facebook.com/reel/1003287998837587) of the strikes shows severely wounded civilians. Other videos filmed by miners show [fighter jets](https://www.tiktok.com/@.818497077/video/7694949327986232584?q=%D8%B4%D9%85%D8%A7%D9%84%20%D9%88%D8%A7%D8%AF%D9%8A&t=1791725176455) flying [over](https://www.tiktok.com/@mohmaedzolo/video/7694930283103063317) the [area](https://www.tiktok.com/@mohmaedzolo/video/7694930283103063317) and munitions striking the ground.

“Just scatter, guys! Scatter!” [one witness shouts](https://www.tiktok.com/@.71119578/video/7695345758152822023) as a plume of smoke rises from the mountain and a plane is heard flying overhead.

Video

[Video 7](https://vp.nyt.com/video/hlsfmp4/2026/10/12/180695_1_12vid-sudan-airstrikes-embeds-2326_wg_av1-1080p/master.m3u8)

![Image 1](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/12/12vid-sudan-airstrikes-embeds-2326-cover/12vid-sudan-airstrikes-embeds-2326-cover-verticalTwoByThree735-v2.jpg?auto=webp&quality=30&disable=upscale&format=pjpg)

0:16

Credit Credit...@Has_Abd125

One of the men described to The Times how the strikes unfolded.

During a video call, Bahar Eldin Hassan said that warplanes and helicopters made several passes over the mine early on Saturday. From about 9 a.m., warplanes bombed the site at least three times over the course of an hour, he said.

About 35 people died in the first strike, he said, adding: “I cannot describe how terrible the scenes we saw were.”

Artisanal mining, where poor men dig for riches at informal mines, is booming across Africa. Soaring prices for gold, copper and other minerals have drawn workers across a wide belt of the continent. But artisanal mining is also notorious for dangers and human rights abuses, including child labor.

Mr. Adam, a student at Sudan University of Science and Technology, said he took shelter in a mining pit alongside a “terrified” young boy after the strikes. “He wanted to run away without knowing where he was going, but I managed to convince him to stay,” he said. “When we came out, the scene was horrific. I broke down crying.”

Footage appeared to show more than two dozen bodies [wrapped](https://www.facebook.com/reel/2326810178143844) in fabric following the strikes. In yet another video, a [crowd is gathered](https://www.tiktok.com/@user1569350715655/video/7695069505411747093?q=%D8%B4%D9%85%D8%A7%D9%84%20%D9%88%D8%A7%D8%AF%D9%8A&t=1791725176455) outside a medical center where dozens of victims were reportedly taken, according a local [Sudanese report](https://darfur24.com/2026/10/11/%D9%82%D8%AA%D9%84%D9%89-%D8%A5%D8%AB%D8%B1-%D9%82%D8%B5%D9%81-%D9%85%D9%86%D8%A7%D8%AC%D9%85-%D8%B0%D9%87%D8%A8-%D8%B4%D9%85%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%8A-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B3%D9%88%D8%AF%D8%A7%D9%86/?utm_source=chatgpt.com).

Video

[Video 8](https://vp.nyt.com/video/hlsfmp4/2026/10/12/180692_1_12vid-sudan-airstrikes-embeds-71769_wg_av1-1080p/master.m3u8)

![Image 2](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/12/12vid-sudan-airstrikes-embeds-71769-cover/12vid-sudan-airstrikes-embeds-71769-cover-verticalTwoByThree735-v2.jpg?auto=webp&quality=30&disable=upscale&format=pjpg)

0:05

Credit Credit...Ahmed Altayeb Abo Ibtesam, via Facebook

Videos taken in the aftermath of the strikes showed what appeared to be Egyptian munitions. One [video](https://x.com/DVSorg/status/2109549407167242559) showed what looked to be an unexploded [Egyptian NASR 400 bomb](https://cat-uxo.com/explosive-hazards/aircraft-bombs/nasr-400-aircraft-bomb), according to Trevor Ball, a former U.S. Army explosive ordnance disposal technician who analyzed the footage for The Times.

Video

[Video 9](https://vp.nyt.com/video/hlsfmp4/2026/10/12/180694_1_12vid-sudan-airstrikes-embeds-1124_wg_mobile_av1-1080p/master.m3u8)

![Image 3](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/12/12vid-sudan-airstrikes-embeds-1124-cover/12vid-sudan-airstrikes-embeds-1124-cover-videoLarge.jpg?auto=webp&quality=30&disable=upscale&format=pjpg)

0:07

Credit Credit...@DVSorg, via X

In June, [Egypt’s military said](https://asharq.com/reports/187558/%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AC%D9%8A%D8%B4-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%B5%D8%B1%D9%8A-%D8%B4%D9%86-%D8%AD%D9%85%D9%84%D8%A9-%D8%B9%D9%84%D9%89-%D8%B4%D8%A8%D9%83%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D8%B9%D8%A7%D8%A8%D8%B1%D8%A9-%D9%84%D9%84%D8%AD%D8%AF%D9%88%D8%AF-%D9%85%D8%B1%D8%AA%D8%A8%D8%B7%D8%A9-%D8%A8%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B0%D9%87%D8%A8/) in a statement that it had begun a security campaign targeting criminal networks and what it described as illegal mining in southern Egypt, near the border with Sudan.

Its campaign included a [Facebook video](https://www.facebook.com/reel/1985299982163879) urging miners to leave the area before they were detained by the authorities.

Days later, several miners were killed on the Sudanese side of the border following an attack by Egypt’s military, according to [The Sudan Tribune](https://sudantribune.com/article/315167) and [witness accounts](https://www.facebook.com/reel/1323773379261200) posted on social media. Some reports said the Egyptians distributed leaflets warning miners that they could be “considered a target for immediate attack” if they remained in the area.

The Times was unable to immediately verify the precise location of the attacks on Saturday, given the expansive mountainous area where the footage was filmed. The Times confirmed that the footage did not appear online before Saturday, and geographic features in the video matched other footage showing the aftermath of the strikes.

The scenes depicted were consistent with local reporting, and several of the videos were posted to the TikTok accounts of miners who work in the area.

“Those killed were like brothers to us,” said Mr. Adam. “ We worked together, we ate together, we sat around chatting together. That was our lives.”

Despite its dangers, gold mining has become an economic mainstay in Sudan during a war that has otherwise devastated the economy. Even after a bombing, some miners said they had little choice but to continue.

Mr. Hassan, who uses his earnings to support eight brothers and one sister, said he expected to be back at work soon.

Sanjana Varghese and James McManagan contributed reporting.

Protesters in India Call for Resignation of Election Commissioner

Thousands of protesters took to the streets of central New Delhi to demand an investigation into the proceedings of the election commission.Credit Credit...Priyanshu Singh/Reuters

Oct. 12, 2026 Updated 2:24 p.m. ET

Thousands of opposition political party supporters marched along a busy thoroughfare in central Delhi to challenge sweeping revisions of the nation’s voter roll.

In a contrast to a week of lockdowns and detentions by the authorities, the demonstrators on Monday far outnumbered security forces stationed on the road. They stood atop orange buses, waving the flags of the opposition Indian National Congress party. Columns of police and other security officials, dressed in riot gear, watched.

The turnout signaled a show of strength for the long-beleaguered Congress party leader, Rahul Gandhi. He marched with a rambunctious crowd, at times flanked by his sister, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra. In an effort to portray a unified front against the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party, Mr. Gandhi was also joined by Neha Bora, a leftist student activist, along with regional politicians from North India.

Mr. Gandhi’s lawyer filed a petition on his behalf in the Supreme Court, calling for an inquiry into the proceedings of the election commission. Its chief, Gyanesh Kumar, has been the target of more than a week of protests across India, by youth groups, opposition politicians, and ordinary citizens who say the election commission’s revision of the voter roll is a politically motivated purge of critics of the ruling party. Since it began last summer, the revision has expunged over 130 million names.

Together, months of protests over a wide range of frustrations about poor education and a lack of job opportunities represent the biggest challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi in his 12 years in office.

The government’s tactics on Monday, allowing the march to proceed mostly unimpeded, were a stark contrast to the intense crackdown on protests over the course of the last week, when would-be demonstrators were grabbed and stuffed into police vans.

The Saudi authorities said they were fending off drone and missile attacks after a weekend of confrontation with the Houthi militia in Yemen, whose patrons Iran offered to mediate.

Listen

· 6:32 min

![Image 1: Abbas Araghchi, in a black suit, speaking into a telephone microphone.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/12/multimedia/12-int-iran-saudi-01-qtvz/12-int-iran-saudi-01-qtvz-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, in Tehran earlier this month.Credit...Atta Kenare/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

Oct. 12, 2026 Updated 11:44 a.m. ET

The Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen was fending off drones and cruise missiles fired toward Saudi Arabia on Monday, according to Saudi state media, the latest in a surge of attacks by the Iran-backed Houthi militia that have targeted the kingdom’s airports.

There was no immediate confirmation of whether the attacks were successfully intercepted. At least 13 people were killed when the Houthi militia struck an airport in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, on Saturday — the deadliest attack on a Persian Gulf country since the start of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

The Saudi authorities said on Monday that operations would remain suspended at the airport in Riyadh after they reported another deadly attack on the facility on Sunday.

Fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis rapidly escalated last month when Houthi forces seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast, taking territory that sits alongside a strategic waterway for global trade and a key export route for Saudi oil. Saudi warplanes have been bombing Houthi positions in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government, as its forces fight to retake the territory.

The Houthi militia has targeted Saudi oil facilities, and it attacked Riyadh on the eve of the WPC Energy Congress, an international gathering of oil officials and executives there.

“The events of recent weeks are serious,” Prince Abdul Aziz bin Salman, the Saudi energy minister, told delegates at the event on Monday. “Our response must be equally serious.”

The Houthis are one of several militant groups that Iran is allied with across the region, and part of what the Islamic republic calls its “Axis of Resistance.” On Sunday, Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, warning that overlapping conflicts in the region had no military solution.

Mr. Araghchi spoke to his Saudi counterpart, Faisal bin Farhan, during a telephone call on Sunday night, according to a statement posted on social media by the Iranian minister’s office. “Insisting on a military approach and ignoring a political solution will further complicate the current situation,” the statement, posted on Mr. Araghchi’s Telegram channel, said. The foreign minister said Iran stood “ready to provide any assistance to help initiate a dialogue” between the two sides.

The Saudi government said that the two ministers had spoken, though it made no reference to a mediation offer from Iran.

The attacks on the Riyadh airport sparked an [exchange of strikes](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/11/world/middleeast/saudi-yemen-airports-houthis.html), with Saudi-led forces targeting the airport in Sanaa, Yemen’s Houthi-controlled capital, according to reports [on Sunday](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/11/world/middleeast/saudi-yemen-airports-houthis.html) in local news media affiliated with the group. The Houthi-run health ministry said that a child had also been killed in a strike on a residential building in Sanaa.

Saudi authorities have not commented on those assertions.

The Houthi militia has been fighting the internationally recognized government of Yemen, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, since 2014. Saudi Arabia pledged to restore the government, declaring war on the Houthis and initiating a bombing campaign that triggered one of the world’s [worst humanitarian crises](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2018/10/31/magazine/yemen-war-saudi-arabia.html). A fragile truce [agreed in 2022](https://www.nytimes.com/2022/04/02/world/middleeast/yemen-cease-fire.html) has [unraveled in recent months](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/21/world/middleeast/yemen-houthis-saudi-war.html).

Emboldened by regional instability, the battle-hardened Houthis have far less to lose against their more powerful, wealthier enemies, even as they imperil Saudi Arabia’s ambitions to transform itself into a global hub of business and tourism.

Many oil industry leaders — including the chief executives of Exxon Mobil and BP — canceled their trips to Saudi Arabia for this week’s gathering in Riyadh, according to [two industry officials](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/business/middle-east-oil-exports-houthi-saudi.html) who were not authorized to discuss executive schedules.

The conflict has stoked further upheaval in the oil-rich Persian Gulf region, which was already [reeling from the economic fallout](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/business/middle-east-oil-exports-houthi-saudi.html) of the U.S.-Iran war.

American and Iranian officials appear braced for the possibility that their stalemated regional conflict could spill back into the open, with the Pentagon drawing up [new plans for strikes](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/us/politics/trump-iran-war-options.html). Iran’s national security adviser, Mohsen Rezaei, threatened on Sunday that if fighting were to resume, Iranian forces would [target digital infrastructure](https://t.me/presstv/210320) in the Gulf, including data centers, cables, and artificial intelligence facilities.

Though the Houthis have benefited from years of military and financial support from Iran, regional experts have long described them as among the most independent of the country’s allied militant forces, with ambitions distinct from Tehran’s.

Iran has been able at critical moments to curb the Houthis, said Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemen and Persian Gulf specialist at Chatham House, a London-based research institute.

When Beijing mediated a rapprochement between Saudi Arabia and Iran in 2023, he said, Tehran promised to stop Houthi cross-border attacks on Saudi Arabia, and succeeded in doing so until the U.S. and Israel launched their war on Iran.

Mr. Al-Muslimi added that while the Houthis were largely autonomous on matters inside Yemen, they coordinated with Tehran on international strategy. “The Iranians know if they want to actually stop it, they can,” he said.

Iranian officials cite the widening conflict in the region as a sign that their Gulf Arab neighbors should re-evaluate their longtime alliances with the United States. Iran and its allies have frequently targeted U.S. bases on Gulf territory during the war.

Iran has been urging the Gulf countries to engage with it diplomatically, part of an effort to sideline the United States as the principal power broker in the region, and drive out its military forces.

“⁠We have always supported strengthening interaction and cooperation among the countries of the region,” Esmail Baghaei, the Iranian foreign ministry spokesman, said in a news conference on Monday. He urged a strengthening of regional relations to create “a secure region free from the destructive interference of external actors.”

Sanam Mahoozi and Lisa Friedman contributed reporting.

**Corrected on**

Oct. 12, 2026

Because of an editing error, an earlier version of this article misstated the name of an event that Saudi Arabia is hosting. It is the WPC Energy Congress, not the WPC Global Energy Congress.

![Image 1: An illustration of a Social Security card with frayed edges and folded corners, set against a yellow background.  ](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/06/business/00ss-income/00ss-income-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

Credit...Illustrations by Peter Arkle

Social Security funds are on track to run short by 2032, which would mean a reduction in benefits. Here’s how four hypothetical households rely on the program in retirement.

Credit...Illustrations by Peter Arkle

Oct. 12, 2026 Updated 12:17 p.m. ET

If Congress doesn’t act, more than 60 million Americans could see their Social Security income drop by nearly a quarter in six years.

That’s when Social Security’s retirement trust fund is expected to run dry, and incoming revenue would be enough to pay only [78](https://www.ssa.gov/oact/tr/2026/II_A_highlights.html) percent benefits, reducing every retiree’s paycheck by 22 percent.

The program, which President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed into law in 1935 during the Great Depression, is not in danger of completely running out of money. While lawmakers have long known they would need to move to close that gap — through tax increases, benefit cuts or some combination — they have been slow to act on this politically charged topic.

But the window to do that is closing.

Many of the lawmakers being elected in the coming midterms will probably be entrusted with drafting reform packages, and they will need to contemplate crucial questions: Who will absorb the costs of any changes to shore up the program, and what will the consequences be? Will people be less prepared for retirement as a result?

Procrastination has been costly, making these decisions now more difficult. Even [some Republicans](https://policyviz.com/2026/09/30/why-republicans-are-coming-around-on-social-security-taxes/?srsltid=AU7gw4UbRSXHIP-WMkoDBUCCeo7RvrL72Cgk2y7TGCj11o18gcDCdy-J), who often resist any tax increases, have recently proposed raising the income ceiling on payroll taxes, the dedicated tax that finances the program, so that wealthier households contribute more.

“Any serious Social Security reform package should be scored on what it does to household retirement outcomes, not only on what it does to trust-fund balances,” said Jack VanDerhei, director of [retirement research](https://www.morningstar.com/business/insights/blog/social-security-reform-retirement-impact) at Morningstar’s Center for Retirement & Policy Studies.

# Strikes Put Saudi Arabia’s Economy Under Pressure

Deadly attacks on the main Saudi airport add to the challenges facing the country, as it seeks to maintain energy production and keep major events on track.

### In today's newsletter:

**Andrew here.** We’re tracking the fallout from the latest attacks on Saudi Arabia, especially on its main airport — including whether the U.S. will join Saudi retaliatory strikes and whether the violence will deter attendees from this month’s F.I.I. conference. We’re also analyzing the blowback to **President Trump**’s decision to allow Russian diesel sales.

Also, pay attention to an essay by **Satya Nadella** of Microsoft published over the weekend about [building A.I. systems](https://x.com/satyanadella/status/2108931348857827686) that prioritize human verification over blind trust. He argues that relying on human oversight is crucial for safety but also says it creates a verification tax — a concept we [highlighted on Saturday](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/10/business/dealbook/ai-verification-tax-rework.html) — that could significantly offset A.I.’s promised productivity gains.

## How will Saudi Arabia respond?

Saudi officials were defiant on Monday after a [series of devastating attacks](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/11/world/middleeast/saudi-yemen-airports-houthis.html) by the Iranian-backed Houthi militia of Yemen, whose government Saudi Arabia backs. The violence included strikes over the weekend on the airport in Riyadh, the capital, that have killed at least 14 people.

Government leaders tried to show that it was business as usual, including by going forward with a major energy conference. But the violence raises questions about how the country’s core industries will cope — and what that might mean for global markets.

**The latest:**

*   The Saudi civil aviation authority said on Monday that operations at the airport, King Khalid International, [remained suspended](https://x.com/ksagaca/status/2109554390504030708) during work ensuring “safety and operational readiness.”

*   The authority said that one person, a Pakistani resident, had been killed in the airport attack on Sunday and that 11 were injured. A strike on Saturday killed at least 13 people and injured hundreds, the Saudi authorities said.

**Saudi Arabia risks being further entangled in the war.** The military coalition fighting the Houthis said it had [intercepted missiles and drones](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-12/houthis-deal-saudi-arabia-its-deadliest-airport-strikes-yet) aimed at Saudi Arabia and promised a “[decisive](https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/2026/10/11/saudi-arabia-vows-retaliation-against-houthis-after-riyadh-airport-strike/)” response.

But the assault on Saturday was the single deadliest in more than a decade on Saudi Arabia, and it followed a recent attack on a [facility owned by Aramco](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/04/world/middleeast/houthis-oil-attack-saudi-arabia-yemen.html), the Saudi-controlled oil giant.

# Duo Share Nobel in Economics for Work on Steering Through Booms and Busts

Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford were awarded the prize for insights that helped policymakers become “better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy,” the committee said.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the 2026 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford, two American professors.Credit...Jonathan Nackstrand/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

[![Image 2: Eshe Nelson](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2021/05/07/reader-center/author-eshe-nelson/author-eshe-nelson-thumbLarge-v5.png)](https://www.nytimes.com/by/eshe-nelson)

By [Eshe Nelson](https://www.nytimes.com/by/eshe-nelson)

[See more of our coverage in your search results.Encuentra más de nuestra cobertura en los resultados de búsqueda.Add The New York Times on Google Agrega The New York Times en Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?cs=0&hl=en&q=nytimes.com)

Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford, two American professors, were awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences on Monday for their decades of research that has guided policies aimed at reducing the effects of economic turmoil.

Mr. Hall, 83, a professor at Stanford University, and Mr. Woodford, 70, a professor of political economy at Columbia University, were awarded the prize “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization,” the awarding committee said.

The two new laureates were essential in the development of a framework that enabled politicians, central banks and others to implement timely economic measures so that there were milder peaks and troughs, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said. That, in turn, helped to shield the most vulnerable in society, who are particularly exposed to economic shocks that lead to high unemployment and inflation.

Mr. Hall studied consumer demand and spending to develop his economic models, while Mr. Woodford considered the supply side of the economy, looking at the price-setting behavior of companies.

Because of their research, “we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” said John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences.

Mr. Woodford said on the phone at the news conference announcing the award that he was elated. “It’s a tremendous honor,” he said. “It’s a surprise but I feel very good about it.”
